extracted.intended_audience: students and learners of mathematics (high-school through early undergraduate) and anyone learning how to understand and write mathematical proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Introductory how-to guidance on what mathematical proofs are, common proof techniques (direct, contradiction, induction), and practical advice for writing clear, convincing proofs tailored to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a proof / what counts as a valid proof
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof is a convincing explanation of why a mathematical statement is true. A valid proof may use only definitions, axioms, and previously proven theorems or lemmas. By nature, a proof uses deductive reasoning rather than empirical arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs must show why the claim holds for every possible case (not just many examples) — e.g. checking many n is insufficient to prove a formula for all natural numbers (the polynomial n^2-n+41 fails at n=41). Use only accepted logical steps and previously established results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal vs informal proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: In logic we sometimes work with “formal proofs”: proofs with a very rigid symbolic structure and little or no natural language. Formal proofs are difficult to read; in practice mathematicians write informal proofs that are readable yet rigorous enough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every good informal proof can, in principle, be converted into a formal proof — although this conversion is rarely practical. Aim for the informal proof to be convincing and precise enough that it could be formalized if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct proof
rubrics_metrics.description: A direct proof starts from the assumptions and proceeds logically to the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show the sequence of logical steps from hypotheses to the desired statement. Example: show square of an odd integer is odd by writing n = 2k+1 and simplifying to 2m+1. Anti-pattern: skipping steps that connect assumptions to the conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a statement, assume its negation and derive a contradiction. This shows the original statement must be true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State clearly the assumption of the negation, derive a logical contradiction with given assumptions or known results, then conclude the original statement. Example: assume n is even to contradict ‘n^2 is odd’. Be explicit about where the contradiction arises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction proves statements for all natural numbers (or all integers ≥ a base value) using a domino-like argument: show a base case and an implication from n to n+1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formally prove (1) base case a holds, and (2) for each n ≥ a, if statement holds for n then it holds for n+1. Then conclude it holds for all integers ≥ a. Provide both the base case computation and a clear induction step (show how assuming n gives n+1). Example: sum 1+2+...+n formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose an appropriate proof method
rubrics_metrics.description: There are several common proof techniques. Experience helps decide which method fits a given problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether direct reasoning, contradiction, induction (or other methods) best suits the structure of the problem. The page gives examples of direct, contradiction, and induction to illustrate typical situations for each method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust level of detail to your audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust the level of detail to your audience: high-school students need more explanation than research mathematicians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide more intermediate steps, definitions, and intuitive explanations for less expert readers; omit routine details for experts. Always consider the target reader when deciding how much to spell out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use natural language to guide the reader; avoid overloading with symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not overload proofs with symbols alone. Use sentences to guide the reader through the logical steps; include calculations, but explain what each step accomplishes. Avoid heavy use of formal logic symbols like ⇒ or ∃ without text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The terse symbolic chain 'n=2k+1 ⇒ n^2=(2k+1)^2=4k^2+4k+1 ⇒ ∃ m: n^2=2m+1' is correct but unfriendly. Prefer a written explanation that accompanies calculations so readers understand the reasoning. Anti-pattern: presenting lines of algebra with no explanatory text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain and justify steps; reference earlier results; number non-trivial equations
rubrics_metrics.description: Every non-trivial step should be explained or its justification referenced; unreferenced jumps leave readers unable to follow the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a step relies on a result mentioned earlier (even many pages earlier), cite it so the reader can verify the justification. Number non-trivial equations to make referencing easier. Avoid omitting justifications to save effort — this costs readers time and causes confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer clarity and consistency in wording over unnecessary variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Varying connecting words excessively ('so', 'hence', 'therefore') to avoid monotony can introduce ambiguity; consistency can improve clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for readability and unambiguous phrasing rather than stylistic variety. Choose words consistently where they have precise logical roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use counterexamples to disprove claims / beware of empirical evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A single counterexample disproves a universal claim; empirical checking of many cases is insufficient to prove a universal statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When testing conjectures, look for counterexamples; the n^2−n+41 example shows many checked cases can still fail at a later instance. Include the notion of counterexample explicitly when explaining why a conjecture is false.
